claim: Staphylococcus aureus (SA) leukocidin ED (LukED) belongs to a family of bicomponent pore forming toxins that play important roles in SA immune evasion and nutrient acquisition.
source: Staphylococcus aureus (SA) leukocidin ED (LukED) belongs to a family of bicomponent pore forming toxins that play important roles in SA immune evasion and nutrient acquisition.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established knowledge about SA leukotoxins and their biological roles.

claim: LukED targets specific G protein-coupled chemokine receptors to lyse human erythrocytes (red blood cells) and leukocytes (white blood cells).
source: LukED targets specific G protein-coupled chemokine receptors to lyse human erythrocytes (red blood cells) and leukocytes (white blood cells).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and is consistent with the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The first recognition step of receptors is critical for specific cell targeting and lysis.
source: The first recognition step of receptors is critical for specific cell targeting and lysis.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the biological mechanism of toxin-receptor interactions.

claim: Crystal structures of LukE in complex with p-cresyl sulfate revealed the location of receptor sulfotyrosine binding sites in the toxins.
source: First, crystal structures of LukE in complex with a small molecule mimicking sulfotyrosine side chain (p-cresyl sulfate) and with peptides containing sulfotyrosines issued from receptor sequences revealed the location of receptor sulfotyrosine binding sites in the toxins.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript (Table 1, Figure 3).

claim: Crystal structures of LukE in complex with peptides containing sulfotyrosines from receptor sequences revealed the location of receptor sulfotyrosine binding sites in the toxins.
source: First, crystal structures of LukE in complex with a small molecule mimicking sulfotyrosine side chain (p-cresyl sulfate) and with peptides containing sulfotyrosines issued from receptor sequences revealed the location of receptor sulfotyrosine binding sites in the toxins.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript (Table 1, Figures 4 and 5).

claim: The conserved sulfotyrosine binding pocket could be a target of choice for future drug development.
source: This work provides novel insights into chemokine receptor recognition by leukotoxins and suggests that the conserved sulfotyrosine binding pocket could be a target of choice for future drug development.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the structural findings.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus is a major opportunistic human pathogen that causes a wide range of clinical manifestations.
source: Staphylococcus aureus (SA) is a major opportunistic human pathogen that causes a wide range of clinical manifestations (Tong et al., 2015), and poses growing health concern due to the emergence of multidrug resistant strains.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tong et al., 2015.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus poses growing health concern due to the emergence of multidrug resistant strains.
source: Staphylococcus aureus (SA) is a major opportunistic human pathogen that causes a wide range of clinical manifestations (Tong et al., 2015), and poses growing health concern due to the emergence of multidrug resistant strains.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about antibiotic resistance in SA.

claim: Pathogenic SA strains produce a number of wall-associated or secreted virulence factors that promote growth, nutrient acquisition and evasion of the host immune system.
source: Pathogenic SA strains produce a number of wall-associated or secreted virulence factors that promote growth, nutrient acquisition and evasion of the host immune system (DeLeo et al., 2009; Oliveira et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to DeLeo et al., 2009 and Oliveira et al., 2018.

claim: The bicomponent leukotoxins are β-barrel pore forming toxins that play an important role in SA pathogenesis by targeting host leukocytes and erythrocytes.
source: Among this arsenal of virulence factors, the bicomponent leukotoxins are β-barrel pore forming toxins that play an important role in SA pathogenesis by targeting host leukocytes and erythrocytes (Spaan et al., 2017), and appear to be promising targets for drug development (Kong et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Spaan et al., 2017.

claim: Bicomponent leukotoxins appear to be promising targets for drug development.
source: Among this arsenal of virulence factors, the bicomponent leukotoxins are β-barrel pore forming toxins that play an important role in SA pathogenesis by targeting host leukocytes and erythrocytes (Spaan et al., 2017), and appear to be promising targets for drug development (Kong et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2016.

claim: Human clinical SA isolates can produce up to five different leukotoxins: γ-hemolysin AB and CB (HlgAB and HlgCB), Leukocidin ED (LukED), Panton-Valentine Leukocidin (PVL or LukSF-PV), and Leukocidin AB (LukAB, also known as LukGH).
source: Human clinical SA isolates can produce up to five different leukotoxins: γ-hemolysin AB and CB (HlgAB and HlgCB), Leukocidin ED (LukED), Panton-Valentine Leukocidin (PVL or LukSF-PV), and Leukocidin AB (LukAB, also known as LukGH).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about SA leukotoxins.

claim: Each leukotoxin is made up of two subunits of approximately 30 kDa: a host cell targeting S-component and a polymerization F-component.
source: Each leukotoxin is made up of two subunits of approximately 30 kDa: a host cell targeting S-component (HlgA, HlgC, LukE, lukS-PV, and LukA/G), and a polymerization F- component (HlgB, LukD, lukF-PV, and LukB/H), which can bind the plasma membrane through highly conserved phosphocholine binding sites (Olson et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Olson et al., 1999 and Liu et al., 2020.

claim: F-components can bind the plasma membrane through highly conserved phosphocholine binding sites.
source: Each leukotoxin is made up of two subunits of approximately 30 kDa: a host cell targeting S-component (HlgA, HlgC, LukE, lukS-PV, and LukA/G), and a polymerization F- component (HlgB, LukD, lukF-PV, and LukB/H), which can bind the plasma membrane through highly conserved phosphocholine binding sites (Olson et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Olson et al., 1999 and Liu et al., 2020.

claim: S- and F-components typically display relatively high conservation within each group (~70% sequence identity).
source: S- and F-components typically display relatively high conservation within each group ( ~ 70% sequence identity), but sequence identity drops below 30% between groups (Spaan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spaan et al., 2017.

claim: Sequence identity drops below 30% between S- and F-component groups.
source: S- and F-components typically display relatively high conservation within each group ( ~ 70% sequence identity), but sequence identity drops below 30% between groups (Spaan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spaan et al., 2017.

claim: With the exception of LukGH, leukotoxins are secreted as monomers that bind target cells and subsequently octamerize into a lytic pore on the plasma membrane, composed of alternating S- and F- subunits.
source: With the exception of LukGH, these toxins are secreted as monomers that bind target cells and subsequently octamerize into a lytic pore on the plasma membrane, composed of alternating S- and F- subunits (Olson et al., 1999; Guillet et al., 2004; Yamashita et al., 2011; Yamashita et al., 2014; Nocadello et al., 2016; Trstenjak et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each toxin is composed of two domains: a central β sandwich called the CAP domain and involved in inter-protomer interactions, and a RIM domain which contains several divergent loops driving host cell specificity.
source: Each toxin is composed of two domains: a central β sandwich called the CAP domain and involved in inter-protomer interactions, and a RIM domain which contains several divergent loops driving host cell specificity.
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge about leukotoxins.

claim: The STEM region is a subdomain of the CAP, which changes its conformation upon pore formation to associate with neighboring protomers and form a β barrel that inserts into the cell membrane.
source: The STEM region is a subdomain of the CAP, which changes its conformation upon pore formation to associate with neighboring protomers and form a β barrel that inserts into the cell membrane (Yamashita et al., 2011; Yamashita et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yamashita et al., 2011 and Yamashita et al., 2014.

claim: HlgA and LukE share atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1) as their main receptor on erythrocytes.
source: Specifically, HlgA and LukE were shown to share atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1) as their main receptor on erythrocytes (Spaan et al., 2015), while recruiting CCR5 (LukE), CCR2 (HlgA), CXCR1, and CXCR2 (both HlgA and LukE) to differentially target specific leukocyte populations (Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spaan et al., 2015.

claim: LukE recruits CCR5 to differentially target specific leukocyte populations.
source: Specifically, HlgA and LukE were shown to share atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1) as their main receptor on erythrocytes (Spaan et al., 2015), while recruiting CCR5 (LukE), CCR2 (HlgA), CXCR1, and CXCR2 (both HlgA and LukE) to differentially target specific leukocyte populations (Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014.

claim: HlgA recruits CCR2 to differentially target specific leukocyte populations.
source: Specifically, HlgA and LukE were shown to share atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1) as their main receptor on erythrocytes (Spaan et al., 2015), while recruiting CCR5 (LukE), CCR2 (HlgA), CXCR1, and CXCR2 (both HlgA and LukE) to differentially target specific leukocyte populations (Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014.

claim: Both HlgA and LukE recruit CXCR1 and CXCR2 to differentially target specific leukocyte populations.
source: Specifically, HlgA and LukE were shown to share atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1) as their main receptor on erythrocytes (Spaan et al., 2015), while recruiting CCR5 (LukE), CCR2 (HlgA), CXCR1, and CXCR2 (both HlgA and LukE) to differentially target specific leukocyte populations (Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014.

claim: HlgC and LukS-PV bind monocytes and neutrophils through C5aR1 and C5aR2.
source: Conversely, HlgC and LukS-PV were found to bind monocytes and neutrophils through C5aR1 and C5aR2 (Spaan et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Spaan et al., 2013 and Spaan et al., 2014.

claim: All of the identified receptors belong to the chemokine or complement receptor families of class A G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), except for the divergent lukGH toxin which binds CD11b.
source: All of the identified receptors belong to the chemokine or complement receptor families of class A G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), except for the divergent lukGH toxin which binds CD11b (aka complement receptor 3) expressed on phagocytic cells (DuMont et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to DuMont et al., 2013.

claim: Human CD45 acts as a receptor for lukF-PV.
source: Recently, F-component-specific receptors have been identified as well: human CD45 was shown to act as a receptor for lukF-PV (Tromp et al., 2018), while HlgB was found to interact with ACKR1.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tromp et al., 2018.

claim: HlgB interacts with ACKR1.
source: Recently, F-component-specific receptors have been identified as well: human CD45 was shown to act as a receptor for lukF-PV (Tromp et al., 2018), while HlgB was found to interact with ACKR1.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge, though no specific citation is provided for the HlgB-ACKR1 interaction in this sentence.

claim: Several toxin-GPCR pairs have been characterized at the molecular level by swapping mutagenesis of divergent regions/loops (DRs) of the RIM domain.
source: Several of these toxin-GPCR pairs have been characterized at the molecular level by swapping mutagenesis of divergent regions/loops (DRs) of the RIM domain, in particular for LukE and HlgA that can target multiple chemokine receptors (Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Laventie et al., 2014; Tam et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2018; Vasquez et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutagenesis studies highlighted the critical role of several DRs located in the rim domain in determining receptor specificity.
source: These studies highlighted the critical role of several DRs located in the rim domain in determining receptor specificity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited mutagenesis studies.

claim: Residues of CCR5 in eCL2 and in the upper part of TM7 lead to severe loss of LukED activity.
source: From the receptor's side, residues of CCR5 were identified in eCL2 and in the upper part of TM7 that lead to severe loss of LukED activity (Tam et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tam et al., 2016.

claim: ACKR1 sTyr41 alanine substitution nearly abolished LukED and HlgAB activity on erythrocytes.
source: Several residues of ACKR1 were also identified by mutagenesis, the most critical being the sulphated tyrosine sTyr41 for which the alanine substitution nearly abolished LukED and HlgAB activity on erythrocytes (Spaan et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spaan et al., 2015.

claim: All of the GPCRs that bind leukotoxins possess between 1 and 4 potentially sulfated tyrosine residues in their N-terminal regions.
source: Interestingly, all of the GPCRs that bind leukotoxins possess between 1 and 4 potentially sulfated tyrosine residues in their N-terminal regions, and the interaction between LukS-PV and the C5aR1 N-terminal region was shown to require tyrosine sulfation (Spaan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence analysis and supported by a citation to Spaan et al., 2013.

claim: The interaction between LukS-PV and the C5aR1 N-terminal region requires tyrosine sulfation.
source: Interestingly, all of the GPCRs that bind leukotoxins possess between 1 and 4 potentially sulfated tyrosine residues in their N-terminal regions, and the interaction between LukS-PV and the C5aR1 N-terminal region was shown to require tyrosine sulfation (Spaan et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spaan et al., 2013.

claim: Post-translational modification pathways involved in the sulfation of the leukotoxin receptors impact HlgAB, HlgCB, LukED, and PVL induced cytotoxicity.
source: In addition, post-translational modification pathways involved in the sulfation of the leukotoxin receptors were recently found to impact on HlgAB, HlgCB, LukED, and PVL induced cytotoxicity (Tromp et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tromp et al., 2020.

claim: A structural understanding of toxin–chemokine receptors interactions is lacking due to the unavailability of high resolution structures of the complexes.
source: Despite these advances, a structural understanding of toxin–chemokine receptors interactions is still lacking due to the unavailability of high resolution structures of the complexes.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: The crystal structure of monomeric LukE has previously been reported at 3.2 Å resolution (PDB code 3ROH).
source: The crystal structure of monomeric LukE has previously been reported at 3.2 Å resolution (PDB code 3ROH) (Nocadello et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nocadello et al., 2016.

claim: Two additional apo crystal forms of LukE were obtained at 1.5 Å (apo1) and 1.9 Å (apo2).
source: While attempting to co-crystallize LukE in complex with peptides encompassing the sulfated ACKR1 Tyr41 residue, we serendipitously obtained two additional apo crystal forms of LukE at 1.5 Å (apo1) and 1.9 Å (apo2), allowing us to build a higher quality model (see Table 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The apo2 structure belongs to space group I4.
source: The apo2 structure, like the original 3ROH structure, belongs to space group I4, while the apo1 structure crystallized in P212121 and features an entirely different crystal packing (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The apo1 structure crystallized in P212121 and features an entirely different crystal packing.
source: The apo2 structure, like the original 3ROH structure, belongs to space group I4, while the apo1 structure crystallized in P212121 and features an entirely different crystal packing (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All three LukE structures contain one copy of the protein in the asymmetric unit and display very similar conformations, with Cα RMSDs of 1.18 Å (apo1) and 0.81 Å (apo2) relative to the 3ROH structure.
source: All three structures contain one copy of the protein in the asymmetric unit and display very similar conformations, with Cα RMSDs of 1.18 Å (apo1) and 0.81 Å (apo2) relative to the 3ROH structure (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by structural analysis of the crystallographic data.

claim: Residues 12–23 belonging to the N-terminal signal sequence are present in apo2 and are involved in crystal packing interactions.
source: One notable difference is the presence of residues 12–23 belonging to the N-terminal signal sequence in apo2, which are involved in crystal packing interactions, possibly accounting for the higher resolution compared to the 3ROH structure (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystallographic data and structural analysis.

claim: The presence of residues 12–23 in apo2 possibly accounts for the higher resolution compared to the 3ROH structure.
source: One notable difference is the presence of residues 12–23 belonging to the N-terminal signal sequence in apo2, which are involved in crystal packing interactions, possibly accounting for the higher resolution compared to the 3ROH structure (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural data.

claim: SAXS samples of LukE were free from aggregation as evidenced by the linearity of the Guinier region.
source: The samples were free from aggregation as evidenced by the linearity of the Guinier region, however, the measured radius of gyration (Rg) increased from 2.41 ± 0.02 nm at 1 mg/ml to 2.68 ± 0.08 at 4 mg/ml of protein, suggesting a slight tendency for interparticle attraction.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the SAXS data analysis.

claim: The measured radius of gyration (Rg) of LukE increased from 2.41 ± 0.02 nm at 1 mg/ml to 2.68 ± 0.08 at 4 mg/ml of protein, suggesting a slight tendency for interparticle attraction.
source: The samples were free from aggregation as evidenced by the linearity of the Guinier region, however, the measured radius of gyration (Rg) increased from 2.41 ± 0.02 nm at 1 mg/ml to 2.68 ± 0.08 at 4 mg/ml of protein, suggesting a slight tendency for interparticle attraction.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the SAXS data and represents an inference about interparticle interactions.

claim: A native mass spectrum of LukE showed a small proportion of dimeric forms in equilibrium with LukE monomers.
source: This was consistent with a native mass spectrum of LukE showing a small proportion of dimeric forms in equilibrium with LukE monomers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the native MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ensemble optimization method (EOM) using ensembles of models derived from atomistic MD simulations yielded a χ value of 0.79 when fitted to a merged SAXS curve.
source: The MD generated models of LukE were fitted to a merged SAXS curve to remove the interparticle attraction effects (Figure 1B), yielding a χ value of 0.79.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the SAXS data analysis.

claim: Rg values of the selected EOM models were in a narrow range between 2.40 and 2.55 nm.
source: Rg values of the selected models were in a narrow range between 2.40 and 2.55 nm (Figure 1D), consistent with the values of 2.32 and 2.43 nm calculated from the apo1 and apo2 structures.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Conformations of the EOM models show a very rigid core, with highly flexible terminal regions corresponding to the signal peptide and polyhistidine tag.
source: Conformations of the models from the optimized ensemble show a very rigid core, with highly flexible terminal regions corresponding to the signal peptide and polyhistidine tag.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the MD-derived models used in the EOM fitting.

claim: Localized flexibility is present in the divergent loops of the RIM domain, and in the STEM region loop (residues 151–159).
source: Localized flexibility is also present in the divergent loops of the RIM domain, and in the STEM region loop (residues 151–159) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the MD-derived models and B-factors from crystal structures.

claim: The three β strands of the STEM remain relatively rigid, suggesting that specific conformational triggers are required to explore the extended conformations observed in leukotoxin pore structures.
source: The three β strands of the STEM remain, however, relatively rigid, suggesting that specific conformational triggers are required to explore the extended conformations observed in leukotoxin pore structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and comparison with known pore structures.

claim: Expression of CCR5, ACKR1, CXCR1, and CXCR2 render human cells susceptible to LukED killing.
source: A wealth of experimental information is available indicating that the expression of CCR5, ACKR1, CXCR1, and CXCR2 render human cells susceptible to LukED killing (Alonzo et al., 2013; Reyes-Robles et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2015; Tam et al., 2016; Vasquez et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Direct interaction between LukE and CCR5 has been characterized by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) in purified systems, indicating a Kd value around 40 nM.
source: Direct interaction between LukE and CCR5 or ACKR1 has also previously been characterized by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) in purified systems, indicating Kd values around 40 and 60 nM, respectively (Alonzo et al., 2013; Vasquez et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alonzo et al., 2013 and Vasquez et al., 2020.

claim: Direct interaction between LukE and ACKR1 has been characterized by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) in purified systems, indicating a Kd value around 60 nM.
source: Direct interaction between LukE and CCR5 or ACKR1 has also previously been characterized by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) in purified systems, indicating Kd values around 40 and 60 nM, respectively (Alonzo et al., 2013; Vasquez et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alonzo et al., 2013 and Vasquez et al., 2020.

claim: LukE inhibited CCL5 binding to CCR5 with an IC50 of 231.7 nM ±0.19.
source: Addition of increasing concentrations of LukE led to a decrease in the TR-FRET ratio for all receptors indicating the ability of LukE to bind competitively with IC50s of 231.7 nM ±0.19, 230.4 nM ±0.14 and 64.2 nM ±0.14 at CCR5, ACKR1, and CCR2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the TR-FRET data shown in Figure 2.

claim: LukE inhibited CCL5 binding to ACKR1 with an IC50 of 230.4 nM ±0.14.
source: Addition of increasing concentrations of LukE led to a decrease in the TR-FRET ratio for all receptors indicating the ability of LukE to bind competitively with IC50s of 231.7 nM ±0.19, 230.4 nM ±0.14 and 64.2 nM ±0.14 at CCR5, ACKR1, and CCR2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the TR-FRET data shown in Figure 2.

claim: LukE inhibited CCL2 binding to CCR2 with an IC50 of 64.2 nM ±0.14.
source: Addition of increasing concentrations of LukE led to a decrease in the TR-FRET ratio for all receptors indicating the ability of LukE to bind competitively with IC50s of 231.7 nM ±0.19, 230.4 nM ±0.14 and 64.2 nM ±0.14 at CCR5, ACKR1, and CCR2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the TR-FRET data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TR-FRET results indicate at least partial overlap between the LukE and CCL2/5 binding sites on the receptors extracellular surfaces.
source: These results indicate at least partial overlap between the LukE and CCL2/5 binding sites on the receptors extracellular surfaces and are consistent with previous observations regarding ACKR1- and CCR5- LukE interactions (Alonzo et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the competitive binding data from the TR-FRET assay.

claim: LukE inhibited CCR2–CCL2 interaction with a better IC50 than observed for CCR5–CCL5 and ACKR1–CCL5 pairs, suggesting a strong interaction between CCR2 and LukE.
source: Interestingly, LukE inhibited CCR2–CCL2 interaction with a better IC50 than observed for CCR5–CCL5 and ACKR1–CCL5 pairs, suggesting a strong interaction between CCR2 and LukE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TR-FRET data comparing IC50 values.

claim: Three pCS molecules interact with LukE at distinct sites, named site 1, 2, and 3.
source: Three pCS molecules interact with LukE at distinct sites, which we named site 1, 2, and 3.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Site 1 forms a surface pocket with Arg263 sidechain sitting at the bottom and engaging in a salt bridge with the pCS sulfate group.
source: Site 1 forms a surface pocket with Arg263 sidechain sitting at the bottom and engaging in a salt bridge with the pCS sulfate group (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Arg85 and Arg290 guanidinium groups flank the sulfate oxygens in site 1.
source: Arg85 and Arg290 guanidinium groups additionally flank the sulfate oxygens, and the pCS aromatic ring packs against the hydrophobic sidechains of Ile103, Leu265, and Phe287.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The pCS aromatic ring packs against the hydrophobic sidechains of Ile103, Leu265, and Phe287 in site 1.
source: Arg85 and Arg290 guanidinium groups additionally flank the sulfate oxygens, and the pCS aromatic ring packs against the hydrophobic sidechains of Ile103, Leu265, and Phe287.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Lys52 and Trp53 delimit the upper part of site 1 pocket and shield the pCS interacting arginines from the solvent.
source: The upper part of the pocket is delimitated by Lys52 and Trp53, which shield the pCS interacting arginines from the solvent.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Lys52 and Trp53 correspond to Arg24 and Leu25 in HlgA and are part of the D-region that plays an important role in hemolytic activity.
source: These residues correspond to Arg24 and Leu25 in HlgA and are part of the D-region that plays an important role in hemolytic activity (Nariya and Kamio, 1997; Peng et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nariya and Kamio, 1997 and Peng et al., 2018.

claim: Site 2 is a relatively flat area located approximately 0.8 nm below site 1.
source: Site 2 is a relatively flat area located approximately 0.8 nm below site 1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In site 2, the pCS sulfate is stabilized by polar contacts with Tyr269 and Arg101.
source: The pCS sulfate is stabilized by polar contacts with Tyr269 and Arg101, and Arg101 additionally stacks its guanidinium group against the pCS phenyl ring, engaging in cation–π interaction.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Arg101 stacks its guanidinium group against the pCS phenyl ring in site 2, engaging in cation–π interaction.
source: The pCS sulfate is stabilized by polar contacts with Tyr269 and Arg101, and Arg101 additionally stacks its guanidinium group against the pCS phenyl ring, engaging in cation–π interaction.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Ile103 and Phe287 from site 1 are involved in hydrophobic contacts with the pCS phenyl ring in site 2.
source: Ile103 and Phe287 from site 1 are also involved in hydrophobic contacts with the pCS phenyl ring.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Ser252 from a crystallographically related molecule stabilizes pCS binding in site 2 through polar contacts with the sulfate group.
source: Ser252 from a crystallographically related molecule further stabilizes pCS binding through polar contacts with the sulfate group.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Site 3 corresponds to a small groove in between Lys 185, Asn109, Asn291, and Ser260 sidechains.
source: Site 3 corresponds to a small groove in between Lys 185, Asn109, Asn291, and Ser260 sidechains (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In site 3, the pCS molecule is mainly stabilized by polar interactions of the sulfate group with Lys 185, Asn109, and Ser260, as well as hydrophobic contact between the phenyl ring and the aliphatic part of Lys185 sidechain.
source: The pCS molecule is mainly stabilized by polar interactions of the sulfate group with with Lys 185, Asn109, and Ser260, as well as hydrophobic contact between the phenyl ring and the aliphatic part of Lys185 sidechain.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Two bound copies of the ACKR1 peptide 34DSFPDGDsYGANLE46 were found in the LukE crystal structure.
source: Unexpectedly, we found two bound copies of the peptide, which may be due to the potentially very high peptide concentration used during crystal soaking experiments (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Residues 34–43 and residues 39–46 are visible for the 1st and 2nd ACKR1 peptide, respectively.
source: Residues 34–43, and residues 39–46 are visible for the 1st and 2nd peptide, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The signal for each sulfotyrosine in the ACKR1 peptide structure is fairly strong, but the electron density of the other peptide residues is weaker, particularly for the 1st peptide.
source: Although the signal for each sulfotyrosine is fairly strong, the electron density of the other peptide residues is weaker, particularly for the 1st peptide (see Polder map in Figure S4B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the electron density maps.

claim: The refined occupancies for the ACKR1 peptide are ~0.7 for the sulfotyrosines, but only 0.3–0.6 for the other peptide residues.
source: This is apparent in the refined occupancies which are ~0.7 for the sulfotyrosines, but only 0.3–0.6 for the other peptide residues.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystallographic refinement data.

claim: The first ACKR1 peptide interacts with site 1 through its sTyr41 residue in a manner similar to the pCS molecule.

claim: The sulfotyrosine - site 1 interactions observed in this study play a critical role in receptor recognition by S-components.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the sulfotyrosine - site 1 interactions observed in this study play a critical role in receptor recognition by S-components.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and cited literature.

claim: Site 2 is only conserved in LukE and HlgA, and likely confers to these toxins the ability to bind the second sTyr of the motif in the N-termini of CCR2, CCR5, and CXCR2.
source: Site 2 is only conserved in LukE and HlgA, and likely confers to these toxins the ability to bind the second sTyr of the motif in the N-termini of CCR2, CCR5, and CXCR2.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation analysis and the structural data.

claim: Divergence in site 2 residues for hlgC and LukS-PV indicates that these toxins might use a different set of residues to bind the second Y in C5aR1 and C5aR2 YXXY motif.
source: Divergence in site 2 residues for hlgC and LukS-PV indicates that these toxins might use a different set of residues to bind the second Y in C5aR1 and C5aR2 YXXY motif.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on sequence analysis.

claim: F-components show very poor conservation of site 1, except perhaps for HlgB, in which 3 out of 6 sulfotyrosine-interacting residues are conserved with HlgA/C and lukS-PV.
source: Contrary to S components, F-components show very poor conservation of site 1, except perhaps for HlgB, in which 3 out of 6 sulfotyrosine-interacting residues are conserved with HlgA/C and lukS-PV (Figure 9B-J).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment and structural comparison shown in Figure 9.

claim: The conserved residues in HlgB might play a role in receptor recognition, although further experiments will be necessary to validate this hypothesis.
source: Given the recently described interaction between ACKR1 and HlgB (Grison et al., 2021), it is tempting to speculate that these residues might play a role in receptor recognition, although further experiments will be necessary to (in)validate this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on sequence conservation and a citation to Grison et al., 2021.

claim: The Arg residue sitting at the bottom of site 1 pocket (LukE Arg263) is conserved in all toxins, including the more distantly related lukGH.
source: Intriguingly, the Arg residue sitting at the bottom of site 1 pocket (LukE Arg263) is conserved in all toxins, including the more distantly related lukGH.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment.

claim: F components harbour a C-terminal extension of their last β strand with an exposed acidic residue that can neutralize the positively charged Arg at the bottom of site 1.
source: Nevertheless, F components harbour a C-terminal extension of their last β strand with an exposed acidic residue (for example LukD Glu296) that can neutralize the positively charged Arg (Figure 9C, F, H, J).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Fast binding of ACKR1 sTyr 41 or CCR5 sTyr 10 to LukE Arg263 of site 1 was observed during most MD simulations, with an inter-residue distance going from ~3 nm to ~0.2 nm within a few hundred nanoseconds or less.
source: During most MD simulations, we observed fast binding of ACKR1 sTyr 41 or CCR5 sTyr 10 to LukE Arg263 of site 1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), with an inter-residue distance going from ~3 nm to ~0.2 nm within a few hundred nanoseconds or less.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the MD simulation data.

claim: Fast binding of sulfotyrosines to site 1 indicates that the clustering of positive charges in site 1 generates large electrostatic forces leading to long-range attraction of the negatively charged N-terminal region of chemokine receptors.
source: Such fast binding indicates that the clustering of positive charges in site 1 generates large electrostatic forces leading to long-range attraction of the negatively charged N-terminal region of chemokine receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation data and knowledge of electrostatic interactions.

claim: Sulfotyrosine recognition through site 1 may be the first step in receptor recognition, followed by binding of the divergent regions/loops to the receptor's orthosteric pocket.
source: This, in turn, suggests that sulfotyrosine recognition through site 1 may be the first step in receptor recognition, followed by binding of the divergent regions/loops to the receptor's orthosteric pocket.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MD simulation data.

claim: Computational models are error-prone and might be inaccurate.
source: Although our models offer a glimpse of how LukE might bind to ACKR1 and CCR5 orthosteric pocket, it should be emphasized that computational models are error-prone and thus might be inaccurate.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of computational modeling.

claim: The timescale of the simulations used is limited and unable to account for potential large-scale receptor conformational changes that toxin binding may induce.
source: Moreover, the timescale of the simulations used is limited and unable to account for potential large-scale receptor conformational changes that toxin binding may induce.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the MD simulations.

claim: It is not currently possible to determine from the data whether LukE-receptor binding might allosterically induce STEM release in LukE.
source: For the same reason, it is not currently possible to determine from the data whether LukE- receptor binding might allosterically induce STEM release in LukE, which would be a necessary step to enable LukD binding and subsequent pore assembly without inter-protomeric steric clashes (Yamashita et al., 2011; Yamashita et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current data, supported by citations.

claim: The proposed models might only represent initial encounter complexes that are subject to further conformational changes.
source: Thus, the proposed models might only represent initial encounter complexes that are subject to further conformational changes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the nature of the models.

claim: Toxin-receptor and toxin-toxin interactions are mediated by distinct, non-overlapping surfaces.
source: First, toxin-receptor and toxin-toxin interactions are mediated by distinct, non-overlapping surfaces, as was also observed for the lukGH - CD11b I-domain complex (Figure 10A, B).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of the models with pore structures.

claim: The initial step of receptor recognition is compatible with subsequent toxin oligomerization.
source: This indicates that the initial step of receptor recognition is compatible with subsequent toxin oligomerization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: The depth of insertion of LukE into the receptors' orthosteric pocket is insufficient to allow the pore's β-barrel to fully span the membrane.
source: Second, the depth of insertion of LukE into the receptors' orthosteric pocket is insufficient to allow the pore's β-barrel to fully span the membrane.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of the models with pore structures.

claim: Receptors might serve as an assembly platform for the prepore structure but be released from the interaction prior to full pore formation.
source: An alternative possibility is that receptors might serve as an assembly platform for the prepore structure but be released from the interaction prior to full pore formation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the structural analysis.

claim: The crystal structure of PVL (pre)pore bound to fos-choline-14 has shown binding of 3 PC headgroups in different regions of LukF-PV corresponding to different membrane insertion depths.
source: In support of this hypothesis, the crystal structure of PVL (pre)pore bound to fos-choline-14 has shown binding of 3 PC headgroups in different regions of LukF-PV corresponding to different membrane insertion depths, with the highest one compatible with the full membrane spanning pore (Figure 10).
evidence: This statement is based on structural analysis of the PVL pore structure.

claim: When compared with the sulfotyrosine-bound crystal structures, site 2 would be at membrane level in a fully formed pore, which would be incompatible with receptor binding.
source: When compared with the sulfotyrosine-bound crystal structures reported here, this would imply that site 2 is at membrane level, which would be incompatible with receptor binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the crystal structures with pore structures.

claim: The 2 other PC binding sites in LukF-PV are located in regions compatible with the level of membrane insertion implied by the ACKR1-LukE and CCR5-LukE models.
source: On the contrary, the 2 other PC binding sites, which have also been identified in lukD structures, are located in regions compatible with the level of membrane insertion implied by our ACKR1-LukE and CCR5-LukE models.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the models with pore structures.

claim: C5a receptors dissociate from lukSF-PV upon pore formation, enabling renewed ligand binding and pore formation.
source: Importantly, these observations are also consistent with the study by Haapasalo et al. which showed that C5a receptors dissociate from lukSF-PV upon pore formation, enabling renewed ligand binding and pore formation (Haapasalo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haapasalo et al., 2019.

claim: The ACKR1-LukE and CCR5-LukE models suggest that the bound toxin could make an acute angle with the membrane that may bring the preSTEM region closer to the lipid headgroups, possibly playing some role in STEM release.
source: Finally, our ACKR1-LukE and CCR5-LukE models suggest that the bound toxin could make an acute angle with the membrane that may bring the preSTEM region closer to the lipid headgroups (Figure 10), possibly playing some role in STEM release.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the models shown in Figure 10.

claim: Sulfotyrosine site 1 has a unique architecture, which is distinct from the recognition motifs used by chemokines.
source: Sulfotyrosine site 1 additionally appears to have a unique architecture, which is distinct from the recognition motifs used by chemokines.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison with chemokine-receptor structures.

claim: The binding site is widely conserved across S-components, suggesting that this pocket might be a promising target for structure-based design of inhibitors preventing receptor recognition.
source: The binding site is widely conserved across S-components, suggesting that this pocket might be a promising target for structure-based design of inhibitors preventing receptor recognition.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the conservation analysis.

claim: Inhibitors targeting the sulfotyrosine binding pocket might be active against a broad range of SA strains expressing different leukotoxins.
source: Such inhibitors might be active against a broad range of SA strains expressing different leukotoxins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.
